title: Single Number
directAnswer: Every element appears twice except one. XOR all the numbers together: identical values cancel (a ^ a = 0) and XOR-with-zero is identity (a ^ 0 = a), so the survivor is the unique element. O(n) time, O(1) space — beats the hash-map/sort answers the interviewer expects you to outgrow.

remember.formula:
result = 0
for x in nums:
    result ^= x   # pairs cancel to 0, single survives
return result
rules: Seed the accumulator at **0**, the XOR identity: `0 ^ x = x`.
The two laws that make this work: `a ^ a = 0` (self-cancel) and `a ^ 0 = a` (identity).
XOR is **commutative and associative**, so order doesn't matter — every duplicate finds its partner no matter where it sits.
This needs **O(1)** space — if you reach for a hash set you've solved it, but not optimally.
XOR only cancels things that appear an **even** number of times. The 'twice' guarantee is load-bearing.
whenToUse: Every element repeats an even number of times except one
You need O(1) space and the values fit in a fixed-width int
Phrasing like 'find the element that appears once / an odd number of times'
You can stream the input — one pass, no storage
antiSignals: Elements repeat three times except one → XOR cancels pairs, not triples (Single Number II needs bit counting)
Two unique elements instead of one → XOR gives a^b combined, needs a split step (Single Number III)
Need the count of how many times each value appears → hash map
Values aren't integers (strings, objects) → XOR doesn't apply
remember.takeaway: XOR is the interview's favourite 'cancel the pairs' tool. The instant you hear 'everything appears twice except one', stop thinking about counting and start thinking about XOR — the same trick reappears in Missing Number, Single Number II/III, and Find the Duplicate.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know XOR's algebraic properties well enough to turn a counting problem into a single O(1)-space pass — or whether you stop at the hash-set answer that any beginner reaches.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Solving it with a hash set or sorting (correct but O(n) space / O(n log n) time), and not recognising that the 'appears twice' guarantee is exactly what makes XOR cancel.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State `a ^ a = 0` and `a ^ 0 = a` out loud, note that XOR is commutative so order is irrelevant, and mention this generalises to Missing Number and Single Number III.

problemStatement:
Given a **non-empty** array of integers `nums`, every element appears **twice** except for one. Find that single one.

You must implement a solution with **linear runtime complexity** and use only **constant extra space**.
constraints: Each element appears exactly twice except one element which appears once
Required: O(n) time and O(1) extra space
understanding: Find the one value that has no partner. Every other value shows up an even number of times (exactly twice), so they can all be paired off and discarded. The challenge isn't correctness — a hash set solves that — it's doing it without extra space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it guaranteed that exactly one element appears once and all others exactly twice?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That guarantee is what lets XOR cancel every pair cleanly. If some appeared three times, XOR would break.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the numbers be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. XOR operates on the two's-complement bit pattern, so negatives cancel exactly the same as positives.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, and it doesn't matter — XOR is commutative, so the result is independent of order.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the O(n) time and O(1) space requirements hard constraints?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That rules out sorting (O(n log n)) and a hash set (O(n) space) as the intended answer, even though both are correct.

examples.explanation: 2 ^ 2 = 0, then 0 ^ 1 = 1. The pair of 2s cancels, leaving 1.
XOR everything: the two 1s cancel, the two 2s cancel, 4 is left standing.
A single element with no partner — 0 ^ 1 = 1.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: All three are correct; only XOR meets the O(1)-space bar the prompt asks for.

approaches.name: Hash Set — Add and Remove
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it as the obvious correct-but-not-optimal baseline, then say 'but this uses O(n) space, and the prompt wants O(1)'.
hints: If you tracked which numbers you've already seen, the unique one is the only value that never gets a second visit.
Use a set: add a number the first time you see it, remove it the second time. What's left at the end?
After processing every element, the set contains exactly one value — the single number. Pairs added then removed cancel out.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass with O(1) average set operations is O(n) time; the set can hold up to n/2 + 1 distinct values, so O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Keep a set. For each number, if it's already in the set remove it, otherwise add it. A value that appears twice gets added then removed, leaving the set; the lone value is added once and never removed, so it's the only survivor.

**Why this is the instinctive first answer.** 'Appears twice except one' maps directly to 'cancel things that pair up', and a set is the most literal way to pair them: presence means 'seen an odd number of times so far'. After the full pass, the only value still marked present is the one with no partner.

**Why it doesn't meet the bar.** The set can grow to half the array before the duplicates start arriving, so this is O(n) extra space. The prompt explicitly demands O(1). Stating this approach shows you can solve it, then pivoting to XOR shows you can solve it *well*.
approaches.insight: A set used this way is really a parity tracker: 'is this value present an odd number of times?'. That parity idea is exactly what XOR computes bit-by-bit for free — which is the bridge to the optimal solution.

dryRun.intro: Add on first sight, remove on second. The leftover is the answer.

java.explanation: add returns false if x was already present — meaning this is its second appearance.
Second sighting cancels the first: remove it so only unpaired values remain.
Exactly one value is left — the single number.

python.explanation: Already present means this is the partner — cancel it.
Remove the pair; unmatched values stay.

edgeCases.behavior: 1 is added once and never removed; set = {1} → returns 1.
-1 added then removed, 5 added once → returns 5. Negatives are fine in a set.

pitfalls: Using a frequency map instead of a presence set — same complexity but more code and the same O(n) space cost.
Forgetting the prompt's O(1)-space requirement and presenting this as the final answer.
Assuming the set is non-empty at the end without relying on the 'exactly one single' guarantee.

approaches.name: XOR All Elements (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'XOR cancels pairs because a ^ a = 0, so the single survivor falls out for free'.
hints: Is there a single arithmetic/bitwise operation where combining a value with itself produces nothing, so duplicates erase each other?
XOR has two key laws: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. What happens if you XOR every element of the array into one running total?
Fold the whole array with XOR starting from 0. Every value that appears twice contributes x ^ x = 0; the lone value contributes itself.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass doing one constant-time XOR per element is O(n) time; only one integer accumulator is kept, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Initialise an accumulator to `0` and XOR every element into it. Because each duplicated value appears an even number of times, all duplicates cancel to `0`, and the lone value XOR-ed against `0` is itself.

**Why `a ^ a = 0`.** XOR returns 1 in a bit position only when the two bits differ. A number XOR-ed with itself has identical bits everywhere, so every position is `0` — the value annihilates itself. That is the whole engine of this solution: any value appearing twice contributes nothing to the final result.

**Why order doesn't matter.** XOR is commutative (`a ^ b = b ^ a`) and associative (`(a ^ b) ^ c = a ^ (b ^ c)`). So even though the duplicates are scattered through the array, the algebra lets you mentally reorder them into pairs — `4 ^ (1 ^ 1) ^ (2 ^ 2)` — and every pair collapses to `0`, leaving `4 ^ 0 ^ 0 = 4`.

**Why seed with `0`.** Zero is XOR's identity (`0 ^ x = x`), so starting the fold at `0` doesn't disturb anything — the accumulator simply becomes whatever survives the cancellations. This is also why a single-element array works: `0 ^ x = x`.
approaches.insight: Reframe the array as a parity question per bit: each bit of the answer is 1 exactly when an odd number of inputs have that bit set. The duplicated values flip every bit an even number of times (back to where it started), so only the unique value's bits remain. XOR computes all 32 of those parities simultaneously in one machine instruction.

dryRun.intro: Accumulator starts at 0. Watch the pairs cancel as we fold.

java.explanation: Seed with XOR's identity: 0 ^ x = x, so it starts neutral.
Fold each element in. Pairs cancel (a ^ a = 0); the lone value survives.
After all cancellations, only the single number's bits remain.

python.explanation: XOR identity — starting point that doesn't affect the fold.
Each duplicate contributes x ^ x = 0; the unique value is left.
The survivor of all the pair cancellations.

diagrams.title: XOR fold across the array
diagrams.caption: The accumulator (shown as the running value) absorbs each element; pairs cancel out.

edgeCases.behavior: 0 ^ 1 = 1. The identity seed makes single-element arrays just work.
XOR on two's-complement bits: -2 ^ -2 = 0, then 0 ^ 3 = 3. Negatives cancel identically.

pitfalls: Seeding the accumulator with nums[0] and looping from index 1 — works, but seeding 0 and looping all is cleaner and avoids an empty-array crash.
Trying to extend this to 'each appears three times' — XOR only cancels even counts; that variant needs per-bit counting mod 3.
Confusing XOR (^) with OR (|) or AND (&) — only XOR has the self-cancelling property.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a hash set or sorting and stopping there — correct, but misses the O(1)-space XOR answer.
Using OR or AND instead of XOR — neither cancels duplicate values.
Assuming the trick still works when elements appear three times — XOR only annihilates even counts.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using a hash set as the final answer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: It's O(n) space, but the prompt explicitly demands O(1). It signals you don't know XOR's cancellation property.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
result = 0
for x in nums:
    result ^= x
return result

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using OR instead of XOR
commonMistakesDetailed.why: OR accumulates bits but never clears them, so duplicates don't cancel — you get the bitwise-OR of all values, not the single one.

followupVariations.title: Single Number II
followupVariations.hint: Every element appears three times except one. XOR can't cancel triples — count each bit mod 3.

followupVariations.title: Single Number III
followupVariations.hint: Two unique elements. XOR everything to get a^b, then use a set bit of a^b to split into two groups.

followupVariations.title: Missing Number
followupVariations.hint: Same XOR-cancellation idea: XOR all indices with all values; the missing number survives.

followupVariations.title: Find the Difference
followupVariations.hint: XOR every character of both strings; the extra letter is the lone survivor.

patternNote: XOR Pair-Cancellation. Recognise it whenever values pair off and you want the odd one out in O(1) space. The same a ^ a = 0 lever powers Missing Number, Single Number II/III, and Find the Difference.
